Across the examples, the stripe was placed on the far side of the pattern extent away from divider 2: a shape below a horizontal divider had an 8 row below its far edge; a shape right of a vertical divider had an 8 column left of its far edge; and a shape below a divider near the bottom had an 8 row above the shape. This compact description is a hypothesis template, not a license to omit exact fixture capture or to assume ambiguous test markers form the same shape.

# Divider-separated ARC panels: inference notes

A solid-color divider often separates two related panels, but the relationship is not necessarily cellwise overlay. Before coding, compare panel dimensions and inspect whether the output is a crop/projection or a recoloring of one panel. Build coordinate-wise difference tables for each panel versus output where dimensions agree, and test candidate correspondences on every demo. For different panel widths, identify the role of the intervening separator column and derive the output width explicitly.

Avoid selecting a rare color and recoloring it based on one demo: sparse marks can instead encode a mask, a panel can be independent, or the panel relationship can be geometric. Do not submit an intuitive candidate until the task program reproduces every observed input/output exactly and its produced output dimensions match the demonstrated rule.

# Edge-rail cross-demo reset lesson

A recurring trap in sparse-marker tasks is interpreting every demo as a common ray-projection problem. Across varied layouts, some examples show marker-to-rail strokes, others fill broad bands or preserve edge bars, and separate rails can make a candidate agree locally while fail elsewhere. Marker recoloring, stroke direction, extent, and rail-band completion are independent choices; don't combine them into one rule without evidence.

For each full demo, record dimensions, rail coordinates/orientation, marker coordinates, and the complete set of changed and unchanged cells. Preserve exact fixtures and run the current saved transform against all of them after every code edit. Use full nested-grid equality, not selected row/column checks. A candidate that matches one orientation or only marker cells is still unvalidated.

If the demonstrations do not yet discriminate a single shared rule, request another demo within the cap. Avoid shape-specific coordinate patches and speculative test outputs. In particular, never treat a plausible output or successful program execution as a substitute for all-demo fixture validation.

# Edge-rail marker tasks: generalization and fixture checks

When edge bars and sparse markers appear together, projection is an attractive but underdetermined hypothesis. Record the rail on each side, its orientation/extent, marker coordinates, output changes, and the trace's precise direction/endpoints. A demo where a top bar and left bar coexist may establish behavior only for the particular demonstrated pairing; do not assume all rails emit beams, or that behavior is symmetric on bottom/right edges. Distinct direction/selection rules can agree on one fixture. Request a demo that discriminates them before applying an unsupported orientation to the test.

Keep the fixture exact: verify row count and each row's width against the source grid before using a transcription. An extra row can silently corrupt dimensions and make validation unrelated to the provided puzzle.

Validate the saved transform against the complete demo with exact grid equality, then compute test output from that program. Do not manually modify a plausible result. A matching single demo is necessary, not enough to infer unobserved geometry.

# Edge rails and sparse markers: evidence checklist

This note captures process lessons from a demo-driven edge-rail task. Its one received demo had differently sized edge bars, two sparse markers, and output added long straight color traces from the ends of selected rails. A first plausible projection submission was wrong. The demo supported only that particular demonstrated mapping; it did not establish a general rule for the test's differently oriented/sized rails.

## Before implementing a rail/projection rule

Record all changed and unchanged cells in each complete input/output pair. For each rail, track orientation, edge, length, endpoint coordinates, and whether it emits any traces. For each trace, record its axis and direction, exact start and stop, cells overwritten, and whether a sparse marker becomes a special color. Test independently whether the rule uses both endpoints or only one, and whether rail length/direction affects behavior. Do not infer from mere geometric alignment that all edges project, or that a collision color applies to every marker.

One example with a top horizontal and left vertical rail does not validate applying the same mechanism to bottom or side rails. Avoid coding a desired test result into unobserved conditions. If a plausible implementation fails the exact demo fixture, revise before submission; if it matches the demo but multiple generalizations remain possible, request another demo rather than spending a speculative submission.

After every edit run the actual saved transform on every complete fixture with exact equality assertions, then separately run it on the test input and submit that output verbatim. Retain the failed submission as evidence that the former hypothesis was inadequate; do not merely tune beam width or orientation and call the result validated.

## Context

The session's initial transform passed the test grid through an unvalidated edge projection and received an incorrect verdict. Later iterations included altered directions and edge conditions without first obtaining exact demo agreement. The durable lesson is about separating rule hypotheses and enforcing fixture validation, not a claimed universal edge-ray solution.

# Edge-rail stream failure review

This instance illustrates how easily sparse markers plus edge bars invite overfitting. Several ray, stripe, and diagonal hypotheses produced plausible test grids, but none was validated against the full set of eight demos, and successive outputs were incorrect. The reliable lesson is procedural: record complete fixtures as they arrive; derive candidate changes from full input/output coordinate diffs; keep each new rule falsifiable; execute the exact saved transform on every fixture after edits; and do not submit until all comparisons pass. A capped demo budget does not license a guess or a hand-built workaround. After wrong verdicts, discard the rejected hypothesis rather than changing one direction/color parameter at a time. Keep one valid action JSON on the final line; `finish` is only valid once success or attempt-cap feedback closes the instance.

The examples had changing palettes, dimensions, and edge orientations, so neither color numbers nor one observed projection direction could safely be generalized. This note does not assert a particular puzzle transform; it captures the failure mode and the checks needed to avoid repeating it.

# Efficient demo-turn decisions

After a demonstration arrives, use the full input/output pair to compare plausible rule hypotheses and identify whether it distinguishes them. Avoid no-op shell checks or rereading task files when the unresolved question is conceptual rule inference. Choose one productive action per turn: request a further discriminating demo if it can reduce ambiguity and remains within the cap, or implement and exactly validate the saved transform if the evidence suffices. Keep the required single JSON action on the final line.

# Exact validation and uncertainty control

For Continual-ARC submissions, require end-to-end validation rather than plausible pattern matching:

1. Store full literal demo inputs and their full expected outputs in the task program or an associated test harness.
2. Execute the saved `transform` against every demo and assert exact nested-list equality. This catches shape errors as well as incorrect cells; output-size checks alone are inadequate.
3. Execute that same saved implementation on the test input and use its exact returned grid for submission, without hand edits.
4. Treat any failed assertion as a hard stop. Revisit the inference or request another demonstration; never move forward with a heuristic merely because it fits one pair, produces plausible colors, or runs without an exception.
5. Avoid replacing uncertainty with a placeholder heuristic or fallback. `NotImplementedError` is an honest signal of no validated rule, not a submit-ready implementation.

# Existing program execution failures

The required library-first check is a routing step, not evidence of correctness. Execute the existing transform on the exact test grid as required. If import or transform execution raises (for example, indexing beyond the actual grid dimensions), or the result violates grid constraints, do not submit a hand-repaired or partial result. Treat the candidate as failed, remove an unsupported placeholder/draft so it cannot masquerade as established reusable code, then gather demonstration pairs and infer a replacement. Preserve the traceback/result as diagnostic evidence; once a new transform is built, validate its complete saved implementation against every exact demo fixture before computing and submitting the test output.

# Verify task-program execution before submission

In Continual-ARC, an existing per-task file is only a candidate; presence does not prove it works on the current test grid. Execute the saved transform on the exact input and confirm the process exits successfully before proceeding. Validate the returned value as a nonempty rectangular list of rows, with dimensions and cell values within the task's limits, and preserve the actual serialized output.

A traceback or invalid output means there is no computed answer to submit. Do not invent an output from visual inspection or manually transcribe a guessed result. Continue through the normal demo-based inference and exact-fixture validation workflow; repair/replace the task file only when a transform reproduces every received demo. This is especially important when a previously saved transform makes assumptions about grid width or dimensions.

# Exhausted-cap retries after rejection

When the demo budget is exhausted, a rejected test output is not evidence for an alternative rule. Do not resubmit the identical grid (or a code path that returns it) as a new hypothesis: feedback is only binary, so this adds no information and consumes another attempt. Revisit all demonstrations and rejected outputs once, recording which candidate assumptions are falsified. Preserve uncertainty if no general rule explains every pair; do not call a candidate demo-validated unless exact assertions actually pass.

Some action protocols refuse `finish` until the task is over, leaving a forced choice while attempts remain. Keep the user-facing conclusion honest: distinguish a protocol-forced submission from a validated solution. Use a remaining submission only for a materially different rule supported by the available demonstrations, and compute it from the saved transform. Never invent validation or repeat a known rejected output solely to move the instance forward.

# Exhausted demos, rejected outputs, and action integrity

When a Continual-ARC instance has reached its demo cap, use the complete fixtures already received as the validation gate. A plausible extrapolation on the test grid is not evidence that the rule is correct. An incorrect verdict rejects the submitted rule as a whole and gives no location-level diagnosis; do not make cosmetic changes to phase, color, or extent and treat them as a fresh inference.

## Recovery discipline

- Preserve exact demo inputs/outputs, the failed program, and each submitted grid.
- Require successful execution and exact nested-grid equality for every complete demo after each candidate edit. A failed command, syntax error, or `False` comparison is not a validation pass.
- If no candidate explains every demo, state internally that the task remains unresolved. Do not submit a made-up legal grid merely to express uncertainty, and do not assert confidence or successful validation.
- Follow only the protocol's explicit action schema. `finish` is not a general abandon action if the instance is still open. Do not fabricate a safe-exit mechanism; continue only when an action has legitimate support and is permitted.

## Session lesson

In one sparse diagonal-pattern instance, three demos showed expanding 2-colored diagonals and varying partial 1-patterns. An initial periodic rule was not exact-validated, and later candidates were guessed from visual impressions. Tool invocation syntax errors and an exact comparison returning `False` should have stopped submission. The transferable lesson is to repair verification first and to avoid treating a test-only computed grid as validated. No specific output rule was established by that session.

# Recovery after demo exhaustion and rejected submissions

A rejected submission disproves the submitted candidate as a whole; binary feedback does not identify which cells or subrule failed. Preserve the exact failed output and reconsider the shared rule against all demos rather than making cosmetic edits to direction, width, or palette.

When the demo cap is exhausted, do not request again. A refused `finish` does not end an open instance. Continue using only protocol-allowed actions. If attempts remain, avoid repeating an identity or other already-rejected output solely because the saved program runs; form a materially different evidence-based hypothesis and require exact full-demo validation before submitting. Do not claim validation without preserving and executing complete fixtures. If no viable validated candidate exists, explicitly distinguish uncertainty from evidence and follow the active action schema without presenting a test-only result as proven.

Each earlier demo request should have a specific discriminating purpose. The saved program's test output must be the literal source of a submission, but execution alone is not evidence of correctness.

# Existing task programs: validation gate

A task-ID filename alone does not establish a reusable solution. Inspect the transform and distinguish an actual previously validated program from a brittle crop, hardcoded coordinate sample, placeholder, or unexplained legacy draft. Never run it on an arbitrary toy grid and infer readiness from successful execution; run it on the actual task input only to obtain a candidate result, not as proof of its rule.

After a wrong submission, the current program's hypothesis is rejected for this instance. Do not keep making coordinate or palette variants from the same guess. Request demos and compare the actual structures, then preserve complete input/output fixtures and validate the saved transform against every pair exactly before another submission. Save the task file only after evidence supports the transform. This complements, rather than overrides, the protocol's immediate reuse of a known validated solution.

# Divider-pattern inference and validation lessons

A divider-separated ARC input does not establish which panel drives the answer. The output may be copied from either panel, a sparse mask from the lower panel, or a projection/encoding across panels. Explicitly compare each demo output with every plausible panel and alignment, retaining dimensions and coordinates; do not decide panel roles from one example or a color-frequency coincidence.

Before any submission, run the exact saved task program on every accumulated input/output demo and assert exact grid equality (including row count and widths). A demo failure is a hard stop: inspect the actual produced and expected grids, then correct the general rule. Never silently edit expected fixtures, remove failing checks, rely on self-consistency tests, or submit a plausible output after validation fails. Recompute the test answer only after all demo assertions pass, and submit precisely that fresh program-produced grid.

# Recovering from a rejected edge-rail hypothesis

An incorrect submission rejects the entire transform. Do not treat it as evidence that only the paint direction or one palette choice needs adjustment. Preserve the failed hypothesis, then use complete demonstrations to rebuild the model.

For grids with edge rails and sparse markers, track rail orientation/location/length, marker locations, and every changed cell. Keep possible mechanisms distinct: a rail may encode periodic stripes while a marker independently initiates a ray. Determine the direction, exact start and stop, stripe phase, marker recoloring, and overlap behavior from observed input-output differences; do not infer unseen cases from a single geometry.

After implementing a candidate, run the actual saved transform on each exact full demo fixture and assert complete nested-list equality before using its test output. If alternatives remain underdetermined, request another demo instead of modifying the test answer speculatively.

# Failed edge-rail instance: cross-demo validation review

A single instance supplied eight demos with edge bars and sparse markers in varied orientations. Several candidate transforms were repeatedly edited using layout-specific branches, but none was validated against the complete demo set; test submissions were consequently unsupported and incorrect. This is a cautionary case, not evidence for a general projection rule.

Reusable lessons:
- Preserve each whole input/output pair immediately; compare every changed and unchanged cell, including marker recoloring and beam endpoints.
- Keep fixture dimensions exact. Validate the actual saved `transform` with nested-list equality on every full demo after each edit.
- Do not create special cases keyed to a demo's exact dimensions/coordinates as a way to make a candidate appear explanatory. A local match that conflicts with other demos is a failed hypothesis.
- When demos are exhausted, distinguish a computed candidate from a validated candidate. The attempt cap does not make a speculative output evidence-based; use the most defensible materially revised rule only if the protocol requires continued submission.
- If fixture transcription is impractical in-turn, request fewer demos only when the budget tradeoff is justified, but never claim checks that were not executed.

This note documents the procedural failure pattern; it does not solve the task or establish marker-ray behavior.

# Failed-fixture diagnosis: stop branch-chasing

A test run that exits with `AssertionError` has not validated the candidate. In an edge-rail task, repeated edits guessed whether the added 8-line belonged beside the divider, beside the marker bounding box, or on the opposite side; the fixture itself was repeatedly misinterpreted, and later claims of validation were premature. One especially important diagnostic is to enumerate all changed coordinates from `transform(input)` and compare them with the complete expected output, rather than only checking that the code executes or that output dimensions are legal.

## Reliable recovery

1. Freeze the exact received demo pairs as complete fixtures, preserving dimensions and every cell.
2. Run the saved transform against each fixture using exact nested-list equality. Report which fixture fails; on mismatch, print changed coordinates/values against the fixture's expected diff.
3. Do not edit direction, endpoint, or projection branches by intuition after a failure. Reconstruct the rule from all input/output differences and unchanged cells; if competing explanations remain, request a distinguishing demo.
4. After any code edit, rerun the same complete fixture suite from scratch. Only a successful exact suite permits computing/submitting test output.

A successful smoke test only proves execution; a plausible test grid is not evidence that the demos validate the rule.

# Sparse marker periods and failed submissions

## Lesson
A binary wrong verdict must trigger a return to the complete demonstrations, not a new palette guess. For diagonal rays, map each marker to its invariant offset `d = column - row`; group colors by offset and derive the repeating sequence and phase from the marker families. For diagonal checkerboard fills, determine which color corresponds to each `(row + column) mod p` class from the geometry. Do not infer `p=2` just because only two colors appear: input rays may encode spacing or additional phase information.

## Mixed layouts
Some demonstrations may encode an output sequence as full-width row stripes, while others use diagonal sparse marks. Analyze each representation structurally and confirm a single transform rule accounts for every example, including degenerate all-solid grids. A branch returning the input unchanged is not a supported generalization just because one demo is unchanged.

## Validation stop condition
Before submitting, preserve complete fixtures and run the saved transform against every received pair with exact nested-list equality. A successful function call on the test input is not evidence that the transform fits the demos. If fixture agreement is missing, request another demo rather than spending a submission. Never submit stale output from before the latest edit.

## Reproduction from this session
The test `[[9,3],[0,9]]` was submitted unchanged then as a two-color parity checkerboard; both were incorrect. Five demos showed both a long diagonal marker structure and row-stripe templates, making output period/phase essential. The useful general lesson is the marker-offset and exact-fixture method above, not a guessed answer for that test.

# Continual-ARC: diagnosing a failed grid submission

A wrong verdict is evidence that the submitted output or inferred rule is wrong; it does not justify minor color or phase guessing. Preserve every demo pair verbatim and revisit the rule from observed coordinates.

## Procedure after incorrect feedback

1. Keep the instance active. Record the wrong-attempt count and remaining submission/demonstration budgets from the new prompt. Do not finish or reuse stale output.
2. Compare the submitted grid against the test input and all demonstrations. Identify the sparse encoding geometrically: for diagonal lines, calculate each line's invariant offset (for example, `c-r`) and associate that offset with its observed color. For horizontal bands, derive the periodic row sequence and phase. Do not assume checkerboard alternation from two colors alone.
3. Infer the smallest periodic rule consistent with all marker offsets and demo outputs. Test candidate periods/phases explicitly against every complete demo; beware that different demonstrations may encode different period lengths or color sequences.
4. Patch the task program, then rerun that exact saved transform over all fixtures with exact equality assertions, dimensions included. If any demo does not match, stop and request a demonstration if budget remains; never submit that candidate.
5. Compute the test output via the saved program and submit exactly that value, not a manually composed grid. Verify shape and allowed cell values before submission.
6. After a wrong verdict, the same discipline still applies: revise only from concrete evidence, and use a remaining demo or attempt only when justified.

## Pitfalls illustrated by this class

- A period-2 checkerboard can look compelling where sparse markers show two colors, but a third parallel marker family may reveal period 3 or another cycle.
- Marker lines should be mapped to color by invariant offset, not merely by visible repeating count or row/column parity.
- A program that runs successfully is not validated unless every demo assertion runs and passes. Avoid printing only the test result while omitting fixture checks.
- Never represent an unvalidated candidate as a validated task library entry.

# Finalization assertion harness

When completing an ARC instance, keep validation checks grounded in evidence. Prefer an exact assertion using the complete received demo fixture and its full expected output. Do not substitute a fabricated minimal input/output expectation as a proxy: if that assertion fails, it may only show that the expected value was guessed incorrectly. Inspect the mismatch and test against the real fixture before concluding the saved transform is faulty. Conversely, merely importing or invoking the program on arbitrary data does not establish that it reproduces demos. After successful verdict, save the demo-reproducing transform at the task-ID path and follow the protocol's requested terminal action.

# Faithful ARC fixture capture and grid validity

When a demo is displayed as a rectangular grid, transcribe every row exactly. Before inferring a rule or testing code, assert both the expected row count and the width of every input/output row. Compare the captured fixture back to the displayed rows, not just the non-background coordinates; shorthand coordinate reconstruction is especially error-prone around all-background rows and row boundaries.

Do not repair a malformed test output by guessing. A submission can fail as an invalid ARC grid even when its visible content appears plausible if one row has an extra/missing cell or the row count is wrong. Validate the exact serialized action grid independently: number of rows, each row length, and allowed integer palette. Then ensure the action is verbatim output of the saved transform, after exact demo fixture assertions.

This lesson is illustrated by a sparse marker demo: a coordinate-list transcription silently appended background cells to rows and thus obscured the actual input geometry. The safe remedy is row-first literal capture plus explicit dimension assertions; do not derive fixture dimensions from a reconstructed coordinate shorthand.

# Fixture integrity and edit validation

During demo-driven Continual-ARC work, keep each supplied input and expected output as complete, literal fixtures. Validate exact nested-list equality using the task file's saved `transform` after each edit. If an assertion fails, do not weaken it to a dimension check, remove it, or claim validation from manually reproducing only part of the expected result. First distinguish a transcription problem from an incorrect separator/panel selection, crop, or palette map; then repair the fixture or transform and rerun all demos. Only a passing saved-file run authorizes computing and submitting the test output. A coding-time assertion must exercise the actual transform, not just independently verify a hand-coded output mapping.

# Fixture integrity and framed-pattern validation

A frame task can be misleading when a frame contains deliberate gaps: the visual outline may become several 4-connected components. Component-only logic may then incorrectly treat gaps as unrelated marks. Inspect bounding boxes and the shared layout before assigning each component an independent rule.

Keep the task input transcription exact. Check every row length against the stated width before running the transform, and preserve complete demo input/output fixtures. If an assertion fails, check the fixture data and dimensions before revising the rule; do not weaken exact equality checks to selected cells or shape-only checks. Compare the complete predicted output with the demo, including unchanged cells.

Test-based outputs are actionable only after running the saved transform on a correctly transcribed test grid. Never patch dimensions or manually repair a computed result to compensate for a malformed fixture.

# Fixture oracle fidelity

Exact comparison only helps when the expected fixture itself is faithfully captured. Transcribe every row and every cell from each received output, retaining full dimensions and background cells. Validate row count and row widths against the supplied dimensions before asserting `transform(input) == expected`.

Do not generate expected outputs by applying the candidate rule, filling only hypothesized changed locations, or assuming omitted cells are background. That makes implementation and oracle share the same mistaken assumption, or can cause a false mismatch. Keep input/output fixture capture independent of the transform; then run the saved implementation against each complete fixture after every edit.

If a mismatch appears, first inspect fixture transcription and coordinate indexing, then examine the transform. Do not relax equality checks or submit a guessed test output. A fixture that is incomplete or incorrectly transcribed is not a validation gate.

# Grid inference and output validation lessons

## Palette and rule inference

A cached task file is worth checking first, but it is not evidence that the file's rule is valid for a new input if a submission has already been judged wrong. Return to the current instance's demonstrations and derive the transform afresh. In particular, avoid assuming the prior task's marker color, background color, or output color.

Compare each demo input/output cell-by-cell and establish:
- which input colors are preserved, changed, or used as markers;
- whether changed cells lie between consecutive markers or between outermost markers;
- whether rows and columns follow the same rule;
- whether existing marker cells remain unchanged.

Do not transfer a literal color mapping from demonstrations to a test with a different palette unless the task evidence supports that mapping. A one-demo fit should be validated exactly against every known pair before submission.

## Grid integrity

Validate the actual output of the task program before emitting it:

```python
assert len(output) == expected_height
assert all(len(row) == expected_width for row in output)
assert all(type(v) is int and 0 <= v <= 9 for row in output for v in row)
```

When transcribing a test grid for local execution, assert every input row width too. A single malformed row can cause a transform exception or lead to a response rejected as an invalid ARC grid even when the inferred logic is sound. Return the exact result of the tested transform without manual edits.

## Cost-aware iteration

A wrong output is only a binary signal, so do not spend another attempt on a small speculative edit. If the rule or palette remains underdetermined, request another demonstration, update the program, and exact-check all examples again before submitting.

# Output validity and protocol-first execution

Two operational checks matter before spending an attempt:

- **Honor the instance's explicit first action.** If it directs you to inspect and run an existing task program on the complete test grid and submit that result before anything else, do exactly that. Avoid exploratory calls or partial-grid probes before the prescribed execution. A failed verdict then means reset the hypothesis using demonstrations; file existence alone does not establish correctness.
- **Validate ARC grid structure.** The serialized prediction must be a nonempty rectangular list of rows, each dimension 1–30, with integer colors 0–9. If extracting sparse marker values, do not flatten and arbitrarily chunk them into rows: derive the output shape and order from the demo pairs first. Ragged outputs are invalid regardless of whether the values seem plausible.

After every edit, execute the saved transform on every complete demo and require exact nested-list equality; shape/legal-cell checks complement, but never replace, demo validation. If a candidate fails, request more evidence when available rather than submitting it.

# Exact validation and payload integrity

When a reusable ARC task program exists but is not yet demo-validated, distinguish these checks explicitly:

- Running the transform on the test input confirms execution only.
- A rectangular output with colors 0–9 confirms ARC-grid legality only.
- Listing changed coordinates or visually inspecting a few cells can aid reasoning, but does not validate the rule.
- Validation requires complete input/output fixtures for every received demo, execution of the actual saved transform on each complete input, and exact nested-list equality against each complete expected grid (dimensions and all cells).

After every code edit, repeat exact fixture checks before using the test result. Do not repeatedly spend tool calls on variants of test-only execution checks while demo comparison remains the missing gate; capture fixtures first, then invoke a concise assertion harness.

Payload correctness is a separate final gate: submit exactly one complete JSON action with the verbatim program-produced grid. Check row count, each row width, and JSON completeness. A malformed serialized grid can be invalid independently of the transform's semantic correctness; shape validity likewise does not prove the ARC rule.

In a sequential demo stream, each turn after a demo should make evidence progress: record what changed, update competing hypotheses, and either validate the candidate against all captured fixtures or request a demo for a named ambiguity. Do not treat another test run as progress when fixtures are absent.

Overlap note: use this with `continual-arc-turn-progress` (per-turn evidence/action choice), `continual-arc-fixture-integrity` (full exact fixtures), and `continual-arc-solving` (overall task protocol).

# Inference stop after repeated mismatch

When a task's existing transform is rejected and the demo set is growing, treat each complete input/output pair as an executable constraint. Before changing code, list all changed cells and identify which unresolved rule alternatives make distinct predictions on an available or requested example. A new hypothesis is not validated by test execution or by a plausible visual output.

After each implementation change, immediately execute the actual saved transform against every faithfully transcribed full fixture and require exact nested-grid equality. A mismatch means no submission; stop tuning individual rows, columns, or colors and request a demo designed to separate the remaining hypotheses while budget remains. Avoid building fixtures that omit rows, compress dimensions, or reconstruct expected outputs from the candidate itself. Capture full fixtures incrementally so later validation is reliable.

This reinforces the core rule in `SKILL.md`: submit only after the saved transform exactly reproduces every demo. It is especially useful for sparse marks adjacent to full-length rails, where direction, extent, and whether to fill a whole line or a projection are independent uncertainties.

# Invalid-grid verdict triage

A platform response such as “the grid was not a valid ARC grid” is not ordinary correctness feedback. Before changing the inferred rule, verify the exact emitted action object against the protocol schema and validate the returned grid: 1–30 rows, each row 1–30 integer cells, rectangular dimensions, values 0–9. Compare the final JSON payload with the transform's actual output rather than a separately copied version. If feedback instead says the submission was accepted but incorrect, treat that as rejection of the entire rule, return to the complete demos, and do not repeat or cosmetically tweak the same payload.

This check diagnoses protocol/payload validity only; it does not establish that a legal grid is the correct ARC answer.

# Lattice extraction hypothesis reset

When a task has repeated stripe or lattice structure, sampling colored intersections is only a candidate hypothesis. A prior task file—even one that executes—does not prove it generalizes; if its output is rejected, treat that as evidence against the transform, not a reason to keep submitting palette/coordinate variants.

Compare full demo outputs with the input structure: output dimensions, repeated periods, marker locations, and color roles. Keep demos as exact fixtures. If multiple extraction rules still fit, request a demo chosen to distinguish those rules before coding/submitting. Only submit after the actual saved transform reproduces every available input-output demo exactly.

# Mandatory first action when a task program exists

The stream protocol may explicitly require an existing task-ID program to be run and submitted before any other investigation. Treat this as a strict sequencing requirement: locate the exact task file, execute its `transform(test_grid)`, then emit that program-produced grid as the sole action JSON. Do not spend a demo request first, even if the saved transform looks questionable; demos are permitted only afterward if the verdict is wrong or the required file is absent. Preserve the one-action response format.

This rule follows the task-specific explicit protocol and takes precedence over the general preference to gather evidence before a first submission.

# Exact fixtures and compact lattice mappings

In repeated-grid tasks, apparent rail structure is not sufficient evidence for extraction. Preserve each demo exactly—including routine background cells, edge truncation, and dimensions—and verify row count and row widths before using it as a fixture. Do not create a reduced/synthetic grid containing only visible marker rows; it can distort dominant-color, separator, and coordinate logic.

For a compact output, map every output cell back to its exact source coordinate or structural feature. Record the rule for row and column phases independently, including any omitted outer rows/columns and treatment of internal zeros. Test the mapping on every complete demo before using it on the test grid. Stride samples are hypotheses, not validation. On a mismatch, stop adjusting offsets ad hoc; reconstruct correspondences from the full demo or request another pair.

Use alongside the exact-equality fixture workflow in `continual-arc-solving` and the coordinate checklist in `periodic-intersection-signatures.md`.

# Marker and recoloring inference

When a candidate based on “fill between markers” fails, do not simply swap colors and retry. Derive the rule directly from all demonstrations:

1. Tabulate input/output differences and list the exact original values of changed cells. This separates marker colors from fillable/background values.
2. Inspect whether changes are horizontal, vertical, both, contiguous, or bounded by first/last markers. In the 5×12 example in this session, only spans of nonzero cells between zero-valued cells changed to 3, while zero endpoints remained unchanged; the demonstrated operation was not an “interpolate between every consecutive marker” rule.
3. Check exceptions: some intervals may include marker cells, other-color cells, or pre-existing values that must remain unchanged. Confirm the candidate on every demo exactly.
4. If rules still have multiple plausible readings, request another demo before submitting. Costly binary submissions should not be used as probes when free local execution and remaining demos can narrow the rule.

The test grid may use different literal colors from demonstrations (or include only a subset of the relevant patterns), so infer roles structurally, but do not assume a fixed numeric marker/fill color without evidence. Keep exact input fixtures and expected outputs for every acquired demo in the verification loop. Ensure every row has the declared width; a malformed input row can invalidate an otherwise sound result.

# Masked-patch reconstruction requires full structural evidence

When a uniform marker (for example, a rectangle of 8s) covers a region and the output has the same dimensions as that region, treat this as a candidate masked-patch extraction/reconstruction problem—not as proof that the patch can be copied from the nearest row or column.

## Safe workflow

1. Locate the complete marker component and record its exact bounding box and output dimensions. Check whether all marker cells form a filled rectangle; do not infer the extent from a single row.
2. Compare each demo output against every plausible repeated instance, symmetric counterpart, periodic tile, or neighboring panel in the input. Map each output cell back to its source coordinate, and explain the mapping across all demos, including varying patch sizes and positions.
3. Use unchanged surrounding cells as negative evidence. In particular, a matching suffix or prefix on one row is not enough to establish that the obscured portion is the adjacent substring; row periodicity and exact alignment must be demonstrated.
4. Capture full input/output fixtures and execute the saved transform with exact nested-list equality on every demo. If the generalization fails or fixtures are incomplete, do not submit a guessed patch. With demo budget remaining, request a diagnostic example; at cap, preserve uncertainty rather than inventing a source mapping.
5. Run the validated saved transform on the test input and submit its verbatim result only.

## Failure mode to avoid

A plausible-looking completion based on partial row matches can output marker values or unrelated adjacent content and still have no demo validation behind it. Generalization across varying masks is essential; output shape agreement alone is not validation.

# Mixed rail and bar tasks: inference and fixture gates

When a grid combines broken horizontal bars with sparse vertical marks, the visual resemblance of their gaps can tempt two separate rules: fill all bar holes and independently project colors along columns. Do not combine these operations without evidence. Across full demos, first determine which gaps become colored, whether projected tracks stop at source marks or at the grid edge, and whether newly filled cells can themselves act as sources. Record unchanged aligned tracks as negative evidence.

## Reliable sequence

1. Transcribe complete input and output matrices directly from the instance; verify every dimension and row width before constructing fixtures.
2. Compare changed coordinates and preserve unchanged cells explicitly. Keep horizontal gap completion separate from vertical/horizontal propagation in the hypothesis.
3. State one shared selection and propagation rule that explains every demo's changed and unchanged cells. Avoid adding targeted exceptions after a failed exact assertion.
4. Execute the saved transform against each verbatim pair using nested-list equality after every edit. If a fixture mismatch occurs, inspect transcription and implementation; never proceed to test output or submission until all pairs pass.
5. If the evidence still permits competing general rules, use the remaining demo request to distinguish them rather than coding an unsupported hybrid.

A one-demo pass or plausible-looking test output is insufficient. Test-only execution does not validate the transform.

# Motif placement and fixture lessons

## Infer the anchor from observed translations

When a sparse marker is replaced by a compact colored motif, do not assume the marker is at the motif's bounding-box center. Across examples, determine the exact anchor offset by comparing marker coordinates with each motif's full occupied-cell coordinates. Motifs can be asymmetric, and a small anchor shift changes many output cells. Record which point of the template (for example, center of a stroke or a distinctive colored cell) aligns with each marker, then verify the same convention across differently shaped motifs and grid orientations.

Keep the original input immutable while generating placements; otherwise an earlier copy may alter later marker detection or candidate eligibility. Consider clipping explicitly at edges, and compare against the whole output, not just the intended stamp pixels.

## Demo fixtures must be literal

A hand-transcribed fixture is not trustworthy merely because it has the right dimensions. Preserve the entire received input and output exactly; assert row lengths and nested-list equality using the saved `transform`. Avoid abbreviated/hypothetical fixture constructions, including replacing incidental cells or omitting marker positions. After every code change, rerun every full fixture and then compute the test result from that same file.

## Response efficiency under a strict action protocol

Do one purposeful analysis/check per turn and finish with exactly one permitted action. Avoid repetitive reruns of the same test grid that do not resolve a specific uncertainty. If available demos do not support a single exact shared rule, request another pair while under cap rather than submit a guessed output.

# Cross-axis motif projection

In demo-backed ARC grids, a solid square motif may determine one full horizontal and one full vertical projection. Infer the exact row and column from the motif geometry rather than unrelated sparse markers. Test whether projections span the grid and only fill background cells. Compare layouts and palettes across demos; inspect crossings with unrelated nonzero objects and preserve those source values unless outputs explicitly show recoloring. Validate exact complete grids for every demo before applying the construction to a test input.

# Multi-demo motif-overlay validation

When output changes appear to repeat a compact colored motif, normalize its support coordinates to a stable origin and enumerate translated placements in the full grid. Test candidate locations against an immutable copy of the input; otherwise earlier painted cells may create false eligibility for later placements. Compare the complete predicted output with every demo, including unchanged motif cells, overlaps, partial/clipped candidates, and color roles. Do not infer a rule merely from shape resemblance or color frequency.

For a Continual-ARC submission, preserve exact full input/output fixtures and run the saved task transform against each with nested-list equality before submitting. A test-grid execution or legal output shape is not demo validation. If the complete fixtures have not been captured or any pair is unmatched, gather another demo rather than describing the hypothesis as validated.

# Multi-demo periodic signature caution

## Trigger
Use when one task family presents large repeated stripe/tile canvases but demonstrations have different pitches, orientations, palettes, and compact output dimensions.

## Evidence procedure
- Preserve complete fixtures exactly; use row and column coordinates explicitly.
- For every output cell, identify its source position or derived feature. A visually plausible sparse-rail sampling is only a hypothesis; do not extrapolate from one layout.
- Compare candidate mappings across all demos, including terminal markers, internal zeros, blank tile-background values, and cropped edges. Different demo shapes may represent the same latent encoding with different geometry.
- Do not synthesize abbreviated fixtures or approximate repeated backgrounds and label them exact. Construct full fixtures and assert exact outputs through the saved transform.
- If competing mappings persist and demo requests remain, request evidence. At the cap, use only a candidate validated against all received pairs; never present a test-only heuristic as demo-validated.

## Pitfall
Repeated geometric pitch alone does not establish sampling phase or output mapping. A regular-looking sample grid can return a legal result while contradicting every demonstrated compact signature. Reject it on the first exact fixture mismatch and reset the mapping hypothesis, rather than layering coordinate/palette patches.

# Multi-layout periodic grids: sampling is a hypothesis, not a rule

## Trigger
A stream task shows repeated tile backgrounds with sparse colored marks on divider-like rows/columns, and compact outputs that differ in dimensions across demos.

## Lesson from this session
The legacy task file was not a usable transform: its fixed-coordinate sample indexed beyond the test grid. Replacing it with successively guessed rail/stride/majority samplers was not justified. Shapes and palettes varied significantly across demos (30x30→5x4, 27x27→3x3, 16x22→2x4) and the test itself was 29x24. Geometrically plausible samples returned unrelated background grids or failed to reproduce known outputs. A small number of selected coordinates cannot establish a shared mapping when output shapes and repeated pitches differ.

## Safer procedure
1. Treat pre-existing task code as a candidate, not a solution: run it against the actual test dimensions and reject exceptions, empty outputs, or unrelated samples.
2. For every demo, preserve the complete input and expected output verbatim in executable fixtures. Do not validate with abbreviated/synthetic reconstructions.
3. Explicitly derive source-to-output correspondence. Record output shape, rail coordinates, repeated pitch and phase on both axes, selected cells/blocks, and whether zeros/background are retained or cropped. Test candidates against every entire demo, not only a recognizable slice.
4. A candidate must reproduce all complete examples exactly before test inference or submission. Keep exact fixture assertions active after each edit.
5. If candidates disagree across layouts or only fit a subset, request a distinguishing demo. Do not patch around failures using another stride, majority threshold, palette whitelist, or output crop without new evidence.
6. If demos run out with no exact candidate, do not call a draft validated. Preserve the strongest evidence-backed code and follow the instance's attempt-cap protocol rather than fabricate certainty.

## Diagnostic signs of an invalid candidate
- dimensions appear by coincidence but cell values are background/padding;
- output is empty or malformed on the test;
- selected coordinates come from a stride picked from visual regularity rather than mappings established by outputs;
- demo validation used reconstructed, incomplete grids rather than exact supplied fixtures;
- code edits continue after mismatches without a new discriminating hypothesis.

This is a cautionary reference, not an endorsed extraction algorithm. The working technique is the evidence discipline above; no universal sampling transform was established in this session.

# No-op retries after demo exhaustion

When the demo cap is exhausted and a candidate has not passed exact validation, do not use a zero/identity output as a placeholder submission or keep resubmitting it after rejection. Those outputs add no rule evidence and consume attempts. After a wrong verdict, discard the whole hypothesis; without new demonstrations, submit again only if you can state and validate a genuinely different shared rule against every complete fixture. Keep the fixture gate intact and never call a placeholder validated.

# Avoiding unvalidated submissions

A transform is submit-ready only when the saved implementation reproduces every received input/output demo exactly, including dimensions and every cell. Validate the actual task file, then compute the test output from that same implementation immediately before submission.

Do not infer a rule merely from a separator, panel size, dominant/minority colors, or visual resemblance. Compare outputs cell-by-cell against plausible crops and encodings. Keep alternatives unresolved rather than promoting the first plausible heuristic. After a wrong verdict, binary feedback does not identify which assumption failed; do not make an unsupported palette tweak and resubmit. Use any available demo request to discriminate hypotheses.

If the demo cap is exhausted without a validated rule, do not replace a prior task program with a knowingly speculative placeholder or identity transform. Preserve the existing file unless a new transform has actually reproduced every available demo. On attempt-cap completion, retain the best validated code; never claim an unverified transform fits the demonstrations.

Before each submission: run the saved program on every demo with exact assertions; run it on the test grid; copy the returned grid verbatim into the single required action JSON. A failed assertion is a hard stop.

# Output geometry and exact fixture gates

A demo-derived ARC rule must explain both cell values and the entire output shape. Compare dimensions and scan row/column sequences to distinguish mirrors from repeated tiling; matching one special-case input does not establish the rule. After every transform edit, execute the actual saved task module on every complete demo fixture and assert exact nested-list equality. A failed assertion is a hard stop: revise the hypothesis or request a discriminating demo, and do not test-submit a merely plausible output.

# Output validity and evidence discipline

At submission time, validate the actual transform result, not a manually retyped grid:

```python
assert 1 <= len(output) <= 30
assert all(1 <= len(row) <= 30 for row in output)
assert len({len(row) for row in output}) == 1
assert all(type(v) is int and 0 <= v <= 9 for row in output for v in row)
```

Also assert the required dimensions when the task preserves input dimensions. Copy/serialize the complete result from the successful program execution. ARC grid syntax requires rectangular lists of rows; a single malformed row makes the response invalid regardless of whether the intended cells seem right.

Before implementing a transform, compare every demo at exact cell coordinates and note all changes. Preserve fixtures and run the same saved `transform(grid)` on every demo, requiring exact output equality before submitting. Do not invent interpretations (such as “extend a bar” or “fill a suffix”) just because one example can be described that way. If competing rules remain plausible, use remaining demos rather than speculative submissions. A wrong verdict is only binary feedback; it does not justify another minor guess.

# Output validity and verdict integrity

Before submitting an ARC grid, verify the computed artifact itself: height and width must each be within 1–30, and all rows must have the same width. A task can accept only valid grids; malformed or oversized tilings may be rejected before any meaningful rule verdict.

Keep two gates separate:

1. **Submission gate:** serialize the exact output produced by the current saved transform, after confirming legal dimensions and rectangularity.
2. **Library gate:** after a correct verdict, retain/claim a reusable program only if the saved transform exactly reproduces every full demonstration pair. A correct test answer does not prove demo consistency. Execute exact nested-list assertions against all fixtures before saying the program reproduced them.

When a candidate is rejected, do not continue submitting the unchanged candidate or cosmetic variations. Revisit whether rejection could be due to invalid grid shape as well as rule mismatch; in either case preserve the exact saved-output and fixture checks for the next candidate.

# Panel and layer pitfalls in continual ARC

When a task presents multiple panels split by solid lines, never assume the left panel is the answer or that the divider is the rarest full-height color. Demos may vary in orientation, panel order, output palette, and panel dimensions; some encode output through overlays/combinations rather than direct recoloring.

Reliable procedure:
1. Record exact dimensions and every full-constant row/column and its position/color.
2. Crop every panel using those observed boundaries; preserve row/column alignment and record crop dimensions.
3. Compare each demo's output cell-by-cell against each input panel, testing direct recolorings, inversions, mappings, and simple combinations only as hypotheses.
4. Keep all demo grids intact in a fixture and run the same saved transform on each. A partial test, a single demo, or a hand-written check that doesn't call `transform` is not validation.
5. If no compact rule exactly explains all demos, use remaining demo requests before submissions. Avoid speculative attempts: binary verdicts do not reveal what is wrong.

Caution: a demo may have an output panel that is a subregion rather than an entire input side. Infer crop offsets and mappings from all examples; do not hardcode a plausible test-specific panel slice.

# Compact outputs from repeated panel grids

When an input consists of repeated panels separated by divider columns and the output is a smaller matrix, determine the output's source rule independently of the panel segmentation. A visually regular 4×4 or 3×N result does not by itself imply a crop, per-position majority, non-background mode, or fixed-index sampling.

## Evidence and validation procedure

1. Verify the complete dimensions and divider positions for every demo; check every row width before interpreting coordinates.
2. Write down the candidate source mapping for each output cell in terms of panel index, row, and within-panel column. Compare that mapping against all demos, including cases with zero in some or all candidate positions.
3. Keep candidate rules distinct: copying one panel, combining corresponding cells, selecting a panel by a marker, and extracting a motif are different hypotheses. Do not use one demo's coincidences to promote a hypothesis.
4. Capture every complete demo input/output pair in a fixture harness. Run the saved `transform` on all fixtures and assert exact nested-list equality (values and dimensions) after each code edit.
5. If no coherent rule reproduces all demos, leave the task unsubmitted and request a demo that distinguishes the remaining hypotheses. A legal-looking output or a computed test grid is not evidence of correctness.

## Caution from a failed inference sequence

For four color-coded panels, same-position majority and nonzero mode can disagree with the compact oracle; even repeated visual alignment is insufficient. Do not turn a partial cell-by-cell inspection into an alleged exact validation. If the candidate fails the fixtures, discard it rather than adding ad hoc coordinates or submitting its test result.

This reference supplements the core exact-validation gate in `continual-arc-solving` and compact mapping analysis in `arc-output-mapping-validation`.

# Compact panel signatures and output mappings

Some ARC inputs contain multiple same-sized panels separated by uniform divider columns, while the target is a compact grid of the panel dimensions. Do not assume the output is the majority color, one source panel, a column sample, or a pooled vote.

## Inference

For each output coordinate `(r, c)`, record the ordered tuple of source values at that coordinate in every panel. Compare that complete tuple with the target cell across all demos. The ordering of panels is meaningful and must be held fixed. Repeated tuples should map consistently across examples; verify this by aggregating `signature -> set(output values)` and checking that every set has size one.

## Validation gate

1. Capture every full input/output pair exactly; verify row count and widths.
2. Save a transform that extracts aligned panel signatures and applies the inferred mapping.
3. Preserve a strict failure for an unseen signature; do not use a guessed default or majority fallback.
4. Execute the saved task file against every full fixture and require exact nested-list equality.
5. Check the test grid's signature tuples against the demonstrated mapping before submitting. If a tuple is unseen, request another demo while available.

A lookup mapping is a valid compact generalization only to the degree that fixtures validate it and test signatures are covered. Do not describe an incomplete hand-created correspondence list as a verified program.

# Divider and panel validation after demonstrations

This session exposed a reliable failure mode in continual ARC solving: the existence of a divider is not enough to identify the transformation. The demos included horizontal and vertical separators, panels with differing dimensions, and several distinct symbol palettes. A tentative rule based on one panel or on symbol frequency did not reproduce all examples and should not be generalized from visual resemblance.

For each new demo, record the separator coordinates/orientation, candidate source panel boundaries, output dimensions, and color mapping. Align candidate source regions to the output and compare every cell; include explicit checks for excluded separator rows/columns and cropped margins. If a candidate does not exactly reproduce every pair, do not submit it or use its test output. When multiple panel interpretations remain plausible, request another demo rather than patching an unsupported heuristic.

Validation should run the saved task-specific transform on every full input/output demo pair, not just a hand-picked subset or a few output assertions. Then run that same saved transform on the test input, and submit precisely the generated result.

# Periodic stripe grids: signature inference notes

A recurring ARC layout may consist of large repeated tiles where unusual colors occur on horizontal and vertical rails. A compact target can encode selected rail/intersection values, but visual regularity alone does not identify the coordinates or sampling phase.

## Coordinate-first checklist

1. Record each demo's exact shape and target shape.
2. Mark complete rows/columns and rows/columns with sparse deviations. Locate the recurring rail pitch independently for each axis and note any edge truncation.
3. Test candidate signatures using explicit coordinates derived from those rails, including intersection cells and rail-only positions. Compare every output cell and output dimension.
4. Keep geometry separate from encoding: test whether the target lists intersections, one rail's markers, or a region's tile-code values. Palette roles vary; don't rely on numerical colors alone.
5. Implement one general rule and run its saved transform against all complete fixtures. If a demo disagrees, reset the hypothesis and request evidence; do not submit a test-only index guess.

## Lesson

Fixed-stride sampling can seem reasonable on the test while entirely missing the encoding demonstrated by other grid layouts. An execution check proves only that code runs. It does not validate the inferred rule.

# Periodic-pattern ambiguity from sparse occlusions

When an ARC grid contains a strongly periodic color field interrupted by blocks of zeros, restoration is a tempting hypothesis, not a rule. The visible lattice may encode more than one phase/palette cycle, and zeros might represent masking, a deliberate shape, or another operation. One input grid alone cannot establish which cells should be restored or how values are generated.

## Evidence workflow

1. Identify the candidate period(s), phase, and coordinate origin from multiple undisturbed regions; do not infer a global sequence from one local run.
2. Separate the observed pattern from the zero masks, recording their exact locations and whether the output changes them or other cells.
3. Request another demonstration when allowed, seeking a different mask location/shape or changed layout that separates restoration from alternative interpretations.
4. Preserve complete input/output fixtures and use exact saved-program equality on every demo before submission. If alternatives remain indistinguishable, gather evidence rather than spend a speculative attempt.

## Session note

In a 28×28 example, a repeating multicolor field had irregular zero blocks. The sole demonstrated output restored the masked entries in that demo, but the test grid used a different palette/cycle and arrangement. That one pair did not establish a reliable general transform; the justified next move was another distinguishing demo request, not a hand-built lattice fill.

# Periodic row-pattern inference from sparse horizontal markers

Some grids consist mostly of blank rows plus full-width, uniformly colored horizontal marker rows. A plausible operation is to extend a vertical periodic pattern: output rows repeat a color sequence, while each observed marker row constrains the color at its row-index residue modulo the period.

## Evidence and method

1. Record each fully uniform, non-background row as `(row_index, color)`; preserve multiplicities when adjacent rows have the same color.
2. Test candidate periods from small to large. For each period `p`, map `row_index % p` to its observed color. Reject `p` as soon as two markers at the same residue disagree.
3. A surviving period is only a constraint fit, not proof. Look for output demos showing the repeated cycle, including enough rows to expose all phases and distinguish alternative periods. Use exact nested-grid comparison on every demo.
4. Preserve rows and columns: for full-width row patterns, each output row is uniformly the inferred phase color across the original width.

## Cautions from a failed inference

- A pre-existing program can embody a plausible but wrong interpretation (for example, diagonal-offset period inference); a failed submission should trigger a fresh hypothesis and new demos, not a minor patch to the failed output.
- A minimum period satisfying sparse test markers can have unobserved residues. Never populate those residues by arbitrary carry-forward and call the result validated. Demos must substantiate the complete cycle.
- Distinct task layouts in a stream may have different forms. Do not apply row-period completion to diagonal or mixed-color grids simply because one demo elsewhere used stripes.
- Keep the full demo fixtures; checking just the marker-row sequence is a useful diagnostic, but exact grid equality is the actual validation requirement.

The row-residue consistency check can be expressed as:

```python
for period in range(1, height + 1):
    phase_colors = {}
    for row_index, color in markers.items():
        phase = row_index % period
        if phase in phase_colors and phase_colors[phase] != color:
            break  # inconsistent candidate period
        phase_colors[phase] = color
    else:
        # Candidate fits observed markers; establish all phases from demos before use.
        ...
```

This is a hypothesis-generation tool, not a stand-alone solver.

# Placeholder draft pitfall

During a demo-driven stream puzzle, a missing task file is not a reason to create an identity transform or arbitrary color-removal draft just to have a file. Doing so risks confusing the next turn's required pre-check with an answer established by evidence. It also consumes attention and can lead to submitting without validating complete demonstrations.

## Safer sequence

- With no existing task program, request and compare demos before writing the transform.
- Keep exact input/output fixtures from every demo and validate the saved implementation against all of them.
- Do not treat successful import, a tiny smoke test, or a plausible output as validation.
- If an unsupported scratch draft already exists, remove it so the next turn will not run it as a known solution.
- Submit only after exact fixture equality and only the test output returned by that validated transform.

This is a supplement to the main continual-arc-solving procedure; it does not establish a puzzle rule or justify any task-specific output.

# Rejected sparse projection hypothesis: evidence-first recovery

In one sparse-marker task, the inherited program projected a full 8 stripe past a divider based on the motif's far edge. It was executed on the test input and submitted without any demo fixture for the current task. The submission was rejected. A later demonstration showed a different operation: an entire column of background cells was recolored to 8 through the motif's central alignment, while motif marks away from that column remained unchanged. This establishes that the initial divider-stripe analogy was not supported, but a single demonstration still may not uniquely establish the general rule.

A subsequent attempt rewrote the task transform using an inferred center-column selector, but that selector did not reproduce the demonstrated output exactly; a first local fixture assertion failed. The attempted revisions illustrate why execution and fixture validation must gate submissions: a candidate should not be promoted merely because it runs or yields a legal-shaped grid. Correct the fixture/program discrepancy and validate exact complete demos first; if the rule remains ambiguous, request another pair.

For sparse shapes next to a solid divider, explicitly compare all changed coordinates against unchanged motif cells, and test competing selectors (e.g. bounding-box center, most frequent column, central motif column) against full demonstrations. Never interpret a wrong verdict as evidence for just reversing the projection direction. In an action-constrained turn, emit only the one JSON action, normally `request_demos` while uncertainty remains and quota is available.

# Post-rejection demo fixture discipline

A failed submission only rejects the candidate; it does not explain which feature was wrong. When the next turn supplies a demo, transcribe its complete input and output as an executable fixture and run the actual saved transform against it and every earlier fixture. Compare full grids exactly (dimensions, every cell), not just whether the program executes, whether the output looks plausible, or whether the test output appears sensible. If the program does not reproduce the new demo exactly, do not submit a revised guess: inspect changed and unchanged cells, revise the rule, and request another discriminating demo while budget remains. Preserve the fixture verbatim so that future edits cannot silently invalidate prior evidence.

# Post-rejection and actual-input discipline

A wrong verdict disconfirms the entire submitted hypothesis; it does not localize the error. With demos exhausted, do not replace a rejected rule with identity, all-zero, or an improvised topology/fill heuristic simply to consume remaining submissions. A new attempt is warranted only when a materially new general rule explains every complete demo and the saved transform passes exact fixture equality.

A synthetic smoke test (for example, an all-zero grid) verifies only that the function runs for that particular input. It is not a task-output run, a demo check, or evidence that a generated action grid is appropriate. Run the saved task transform on the actual provided test grid and submit that exact result. If no validated transform exists, do not claim validation; adhere to the active action protocol without treating legality or execution as correctness evidence.

# Post-verdict action selection when demos are exhausted

A failed submission invalidates the hypothesis behind that grid; it does not supply cell-level diagnostics. Do not respond by reflexively sending another demo request after the cap is already reached, nor by repeating a previously rejected grid with cosmetic edits.

## Recovery sequence

1. Read the latest protocol counters before choosing an action. Track wrong submissions and demo requests from the current feedback, not from a stale summary or earlier counter.
2. If a demo request was refused, record that the demo budget is exhausted. Do not issue another request; the refusal is not a new example and yields no transformation evidence.
3. Reconstruct and compare the complete demo pairs from the current task conversation. For a materially new candidate, state the changed coordinates and why each change follows from the demos; explicitly compare against prior failed outputs.
4. If an exact general transform cannot be validated, do not describe a guess as validated. The action schema may still require a submission while the instance remains active; avoid `finish` unless the protocol says the instance is over. If forced to submit, choose only a materially revised hypothesis, and compute the output from the saved task transform rather than hand-authoring a grid.
5. Once feedback says the attempt cap is reached and the instance is over, preserve a program only if it exactly matched every complete demo. Otherwise leave the prior file unchanged, then issue the required finish action.

## Cautions

- An exhausted-budget request can consume turns without increasing information; check counters first.
- A budget of multiple attempts is not permission to cycle through arbitrary guesses. Each retry should be a falsifiable, demo-supported rule, validated across all fixtures.
- Keep the final response to exactly one permitted action JSON when the ARC protocol requires it.

# Post-verdict reset for sparse edge-bar puzzles

A plausible edge-bar “ray” hypothesis is not validated merely because it explains one output segment. In the task reviewed here, boundary bars changed orientation and length across demos; output varied in which endpoint projected, projected width/extent, and whether marker pixels became color 4. The initially inferred uniform inward beam failed on the test despite appearing plausible.

## Reusable recovery procedure

1. After any incorrect submission, treat the whole rule hypothesis as disproven. Do not make a cosmetic change to the failed output.
2. For each demo, list all changed coordinates with input→output values, and separately record unchanged bars, sparse markers, and background.
3. Compare candidate mechanisms across all demonstrations: endpoint-specific rays, whole-bar projections, marker-template overlays, and orientations. Explain both the painted cells and the conspicuous cells that remain unchanged.
4. Encode the candidate in the saved task transform and build literal complete fixtures. Execute the same saved transform on every fixture and require exact nested-list equality before submitting.
5. If no candidate fits every full pair, request another demo while available. A test-grid execution or hand-derived output is not evidence of demo agreement.

## Pitfall

Do not infer projection width, direction, collision behavior, or marker recoloring from a single visually aligned stripe. These are separate rule components and each needs support across examples. A binary wrong verdict gives no diagnostic detail, so preserve attempts by validating first.

When a demo cap remains, seek an example that distinguishes the competing explanations. Another submission is appropriate only after the saved transform passes exact nested-list assertions for every received demo and its test output is freshly computed. Competing rules can include projection at every marker, projection only for selected colors, nearest-marker propagation, and fills bounded by other marks.

Before applying such a hypothesis to a test with repeated same-color markers, varying gaps, or a different grid height, seek a pair that distinguishes those alternatives.
